title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
text:
It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.
Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
The Neets review has taken on a life of its own. ITV has commissioned a four-part docudrama on the writing of the report. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Neets: The Musical will be opening just before Christmas. And Mud’s classic, That’s Neet, That’s Neet, I Really Love Your Tiger Feet is the hot favourite to be the UK’s entry for next year’s Eurovision. At long last, a song we can all get behind and that has a realistic chance of winning.
But Tuesday was the day. The day Big Al took centre stage at Google HQ to tell us he was about to tell us everything he had already told us. We just had to listen quietly and bathe in his reflected glory. And tick off all the review’s highlights as they were mentioned. Neets bingo. We were in danger of creating a lost generation. In fact we already might have done, as more than 10% of young people under 25 had been out of work, education or training for more than 20 years.
It wasn’t that young people were lazy snowflakes. They had been let down. Time now to invest in this generation, not write them off. To invest in their futures like other northern European countries do. You couldn’t get hundreds of thousands of people back to work just by cutting benefits. That was delusional. Rather, a culture shift was needed. A recalibration of the way the state engaged with an abandoned generation.
Almost seamlessly, the venue shifted to the Commons where Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, surrounded by Andy Burnham and most of the cabinet, was due to give his own 10-minute potted version of the Milburn review. First though, an intervention from the speaker, who wanted to put on record his concern that copies of the report hadn’t been laid before the house. Not that anyone needed a copy; we all knew it off by heart.
Pat then repeated pretty much everything Milburn had said an hour earlier. The only difference being that McFadden managed to sound a bit gloomier about the whole thing. Not because he wasn’t enthusiastic, but because he was. The more engaged and upbeat Pat is, the more depressed he sounds. It’s just the way he’s wired. Gloom is his natural state of being.
Even with McFadden’s rather downbeat delivery, this still felt like quite a moment. For the last two and a half years, many have criticised the government for its lack of vision. For lurching from one crisis to the next. Here, at last, was that vision. A major shift in the way the state would engage with a generation of young people who hitherto had been ignored or left on benefits. You couldn’t help feeling a bit sorry for Keir Starmer. He was the one who – albeit late in the day – had commissioned the review, but Burnham would get the credit. That’s showbiz for you.
While Labour benches were packed, barely a dozen Tory backbench MPs had bothered to come for what might be a seismic shift in policy. Maybe they are the snowflakes. Or maybe they really aren’t that bothered that so many young people feel they have no future. Or maybe they couldn’t face sitting through the truly hopeless response of the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately.
You really can’t blame so many Neets for feeling the odds are stacked against them when they see the rise and rise of Whately. Helen is everything the Tories believe Neets to be. Lazy, stupid. A woman without principle who has morphed into whatever shape is required to fit in with a Tory party sliding ever further to the right. If there were any justice, Whately would be one of the many people struggling to find a decent job. Or any job. Had she been born 25 years later, it would have been Helen claiming benefits.
Her reply was one of the most half-witted imaginable. You can just about forgive the nastiness. That comes with the Tory territory. So of course she was demanding that billions more be cut from benefits. Because that’s the only language they think Neets understand. What was too much was the stupidity. Only Whately could claim that Milburn was just following Tory policy in the same breath as declaring it was a Labour benefits bonanza.
The rest of the session passed with little incident. A few Labour backbenchers gently reminded Gloomy Pat that while they were fully behind most of the review they were concerned that some young people might lose out on benefits. A warning shot. This was a battle to be fought over later. Suella Braverman managed to take off her handcuffs for a few minutes – like most Reform MPs she is being paid a fortune to be chained to Katie Price – to ask about immigrants. No one paid her any attention.
Where this goes from here is anyone’s guess. Will the new jobs exist or become Milburn’s Potemkin village? It could be that in 10 years’ time, we will look back and see this as the moment society reshaped its attitudes to young people. Or it could just get forgotten, filed away under “too difficult”. A road to hell paved with good intentions. But hey! We will always have Eurovision. And Neets! Might even get transferred to Broadway.
